summary: This note is a general overview of biological evolution, defined as change in heritable characteristics of populations over generations, driven by processes such as natural selection, genetic drift, mutation and gene flow. It covers the Darwin-Wallace theory of natural selection and its observable premises, the genetic basis of inheritance (DNA, genes, alleles, phenotype versus genotype), and the sources of new variation, including mutation, gene duplication, sexual recombination and horizontal gene transfer. It also discusses drift, neutral theory, mutation bias, linkage and genetic hitchhiking, sexual selection, micro- versus macroevolution, adaptation, vestigial structures and exaptation. The text ends abruptly mid-sentence while introducing exaptation.
one_line: Overview of biological evolution covering natural selection, genetic drift, mutation, gene flow, inheritance, adaptation and speciation.
key_facts: Evolution is defined as the change in the heritable characteristics of biological populations over successive generations.
The theory of evolution by natural selection was conceived independently by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace in the mid-19th century.
The theory was first set out in detail in Darwin's book On the Origin of Species.
All life on Earth shares a last universal common ancestor (LUCA), which lived approximately 3.5-3.8 billion years ago.
Mutations are the ultimate source of genetic variation in all organisms.
About half of the mutations in the coding regions of protein-coding genes are deleterious, and the other half are neutral.
The two-fold cost of sex was first described by John Maynard Smith.
The rate of recombination is low, approximately two events per chromosome per generation.
Horizontal gene transfer is most common among bacteria and contributes to the spread of antibiotic resistance in medicine.
Genetic drift is the random fluctuation of allele frequencies within a population from one generation to the next.

Haldane and Fisher argued that mutation is a weak pressure easily overcome by selection, so mutation tendencies would be ineffectual except under neutral evolution or extraordinarily high mutation rates.
Eugene Odum, a founder of ecology, defined an ecosystem as any unit including all of the organisms in a given area interacting with the physical environment.
The bacterium Escherichia coli evolved the ability to use citric acid as a nutrient in a long-term laboratory experiment.
The overwhelming majority of species are microscopic prokaryotes, which form about half the world's biomass.
Macroevolution is the outcome of long periods of microevolution, so the distinction between them is simply the time involved.
